The Japanese black seaperch Sebastes ventricosus is a viviparous scorpaenid that exhibits distinct size-related life history milestones. Analyses of total length data indicate that individuals ultimately attain a maximum total length of 25 centimeters [Li = 25 centimeters], a value consistent with congeners inhabiting temperate rocky reefs. Females mature at a considerably smaller size, with total length at puberty estimated at 12 cm [Lp = 12 cm], marking the onset of reproductive capability. The wet weight at puberty, derived from length-weight relationships, is approximately 21.6 grams [Wwp = approximately 21.6 grams], reflecting the substantial somatic growth that precedes initial reproduction. The physiological costs of this early investment are balanced by a protracted growth trajectory toward the ultimate adult body mass, which reaches 209 grams [Wwi = 209 grams]. Collectively, these metrics define a life history strategy characterized by moderate size and delayed maturity relative to smaller-bodied sebastid species.

Reproductive output in Sebastes ventricosus is tightly regulated by water temperature, with field observations conducted at 17.3 °C [T = 17.3 °C] revealing a maximum reproduction rate of approximately 55 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 55 offspring per day] derived from fecundity data. The incubation of yolk-laden eggs within the maternal ovary proceeds throughout a prolonged gestation, with the chorionate embryos developing endogenously before parturition. This high fecundity is typical of viviparous scorpaenids that experience high larval mortality during the pelagic larval phase. The temperature-dependence of this reproductive output underscores the importance of thermal habitat in shaping annual recruitment potential for this species.

The early life stages of Sebastes ventricosus are characterised by a very modest initial mass at parturition. Newborn larvae emerge from the maternal brood cavity weighing approximately 0.000268 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000268 grams], a value calculated from the mean egg diameter of 0.8 millimeters, though the species is viviparous. This minute starting mass places the species among the smaller offspring producers within the genus, reflecting the trade-off between larval size and fecundity. The yolk-sac larva depends entirely on lecithotrophic resources during the first days following eclosion from the chorion. Rapid yolk absorption precedes the onset of exogenous feeding, at which point the exotrophic transition to active prey capture begins. The energetic demands of this early growth phase are substantial, necessitating high prey densities in the pelagic environment to support the developing pre-metamorphic larva.

Lifespan data for Sebastes ventricosus indicate a maximum longevity of 20 years [am = 20 years] under natural thermal conditions of 17.3 °C [T = 17.3 °C]. This extended lifespan is characteristic of many temperate Sebastes species and reflects a slow-paced life history with iteroparous reproduction across multiple seasons. The age-related increase in reproductive experience may confer advantages in larval provisioning, as older females often produce higher quality offspring. Field recapture studies confirm that individuals can survive for over two decades, with senescent mortality occurring gradually rather than abruptly following reproductive senescence. The relatively high longevity suggests that adult survival contributes significantly to population stability, buffering against years of poor recruitment caused by unfavourable oceanographic conditions. This lifespan, coupled with the moderate adult body mass of 209 grams [Wwi = 209 grams], positions the species within a slow life history continuum.

Comparative examination of length and weight at puberty reveals a coherent allometric relationship in Sebastes ventricosus. The total length at puberty of 12 cm [Lp = 12 cm] corresponds to approximately 48 percent of the ultimate total length of 25 centimeters [Li = 25 centimeters], a ratio common among iteroparous scorpaenids. The wet weight at puberty of 21.6 grams [Wwp = 21.6 grams] represents roughly 10 percent of the ultimate wet weight of 209 grams [Wwi = 209 grams], indicating that individuals allocate considerable somatic growth after maturity to approach their asymptotic size. This pattern of early maturity at a relatively small size, followed by substantial post-pubertal growth, is associated with the need to achieve reproductive output quickly while continuing to increase fecundity with age. Such a strategy is favoured in environments where adult survival is relatively predictable and where reproductive success scales positively with female body size and age.
